bill.title: A joint resolution providing for congressional disapproval of the proposed foreign military sale to the Government of Israel of certain defense articles and services.
bill.latestActionText: Motion to discharge Senate Committee on Foreign Relations rejected by Yea-Nay Vote. 40 - 59. Record Vote Number: 80. (consideration: CR S1764-1779)
bill.officialSummary: This joint resolution prohibits a proposed foreign military sale of certain defense articles and services to Israel.

classification.plainSummary: This joint resolution would block a proposed sale of military equipment and services to the government of Israel. Under the Arms Export Control Act, Congress has the authority to disapprove foreign military sales through such a resolution. If enacted, this specific sale would not proceed.

industries.rationale: The resolution directly blocks a foreign military sale, affecting defense contractors who would supply the articles and services.

plain.whatItDoes: This joint resolution would ban a proposed foreign military sale of certain defense articles and services to Israel.
plain.whoItTouches: Mostly people outside the United States. It reaches most readers here only indirectly.
plain.everydayEffect: If it passed, the change would show up in what the United States does abroad. Nothing has changed yet. Most bills never become law.
plain.source: Reworded from the official summary. Staff at the Congressional Research Service wrote that summary. It is public domain, and the full text of it is further down this page.

method.formula: score = Σ_industries ( donorShare(industry) × billWeight(industry) ), where billWeight = classifierConfidence / Σ classifierConfidence. Range 0–1, read as a weighted share of disclosed itemized money.

ordinary.text: They wrote this bill. Sponsoring a bill about your own district's industry is the ordinary case, not the odd one.

disclaimer: This tool places two public records next to each other: who donated to a member of Congress, and what that member legislated on. Any overlap you see is a correlation, not causation. It is not evidence of a quid pro quo, of influence, or of wrongdoing. Legislators routinely receive support from industries in their district for the same reason they legislate on them: those industries are there.
